title: A rope of loose thread
hookLine: a boat hauled across the sea on a rope of loose thread, and water seeping from an unbaked cup: Lal Ded admits she might not make it
carry: across samsara's sea, we ask to be carried

lines: A BOAT ON A ROPE OF THREAD.
cards: A cup shaped from wet clay and dried in the sun, but never fired in a kiln. It looks like a cup. It holds its shape.
Pour water in, though, and the sides darken. Drop by drop, the water soaks into the clay and seeps away, and the cup begins to soften.
In one saying Lal Ded uses that kind of cup to describe herself, next to an even shakier picture: a boat, a whole sea, and a rope of loose thread.

teach.b: Here is the vakh, in paraphrase.
With a rope of loose, untwisted thread, I am hauling a boat across the sea. If only God would hear me and carry me over.
Like water in cups of unbaked clay, I am seeping away.
How I long to go home. First the rope. Towing a heavy boat across the sea with untwisted thread is close to hopeless.
The rope is whatever she has to pull with: her effort, her discipline, her practice. She doesn't pretend it's strong. Then the prayer in the middle: if only God would hear me.

She isn't boasting that she's arrived. She's asking to be carried. Many readers hear in her sea one of Hinduism's oldest pictures: samsara, life after life, as an ocean, and God as the one who carries you across.
Then the cup, her life draining away a little each day, the way water leaves unfired clay. Then the last word, home. Not the house she left.
Some Shaiva readers in Kashmir hear the self finding its way back to Shiva, its true home; some hear, more simply, the ache to be where you belong. And notice the honesty.
The woman who danced free on one word says plainly: my rope is weak, my time is leaking, I may not make it across on my own. The tradition kept this saying. It didn't polish it into a victory.
It let a saint say she was struggling.

how: Lal Ded's vakhs, including this one, are recited and sung in Kashmiri, and Kashmiris quote her lines in everyday speech.

o: a poet who wrote only of victory over every hardship
a Kashmiri boatwoman who ferried pilgrims across a lake
a Kashmiri saint who sang honestly of struggle and longing

games.q: Lal Ded's three pictures — tap the pairs.
p: how I long to go home

s: in this vakh, Lal Ded says her rope is strong enough
she says it's loose, untwisted thread, and asks God to carry her over.
she compares herself to water in cups of unbaked clay
her life seeps away, a little at a time.
many readers hear her sea as samsara, the round of life after life
and God as the one who carries you across it, a prayer bhajans still sing.

games.q: you're Lal Ded in the vakh. the boat is heavy, the sea is wide, and your rope is loose thread. what do you do?
o: cut the rope and let the boat drift.
keep pulling, and ask God to carry you over.
say the rope is stronger than it is.
games.why: she keeps hauling and asks to be heard and carried. she never pretends the rope is strong.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're trying to pull across a wide stretch of water, a habit, a hard conversation, a hope, and look without blame at what you're pulling with, thin or frayed; then keep pulling anyway.

If you pray, you can ask in your own words to be carried the rest of the way. And if the rope ever feels too thin to hold, you don't have to pull alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Lal Ded. The poet hauling a boat with loose thread, seeping away like water in unbaked clay, and still longing for home. Today's word.

orig.note: vakh, the Kashmiri name for Lal Ded's short sayings, here written in Devanagari.

carryVoice: Your line: across samsara's sea, we ask to be carried. Loose thread, and still the longing for home. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Lal Ded, vakh of the boat towed with untwisted thread and the cups of unbaked clay
Hindu image of samsara as an ocean (bhava-sagara) that God carries the devotee across, common in bhajans
